explore_prose: Each row below is one BLIS replay run. The load axis is session-tree lanes, not in-flight requests: one lane drives a whole agent trajectory that fans out into many sub-requests, so a lane is worth far more concurrency than a single chat turn.
The interactivity floor is the default 50 tok/s per user (ITL p99 ≤ 20 ms).

glossary.def: One live agent trajectory, not one request.
glossary.long: An AgentX lane replays a whole recorded coding session: a main turn, its sub-agent groups and their inner requests. One lane therefore puts many requests in flight, which is why the lane ladder is much shorter than a request-concurrency ramp.

glossary.def: tp × pcp × dp — derived, never declared.
glossary.long: A width of 1 shards no experts, so it neither saves memory nor costs collectives. This is why adding dp rescues a layout that failed at the same tp.

glossary.def: C* is the highest load meeting the floor; the recommendation is 0.8 × C*.
glossary.long: The reported figures are measured AT the usable load, not read off a nearby rung of the ladder, so the throughput quoted is the throughput at the load recommended.

glossary.def: About 99 input tokens per output token on this corpus.
glossary.long: Output tok/s per GPU is the ranking metric but a poor description of the machine's work here: most of each request is reading context, so a low output rate can coexist with very high total token throughput.

hero.html: Every expert-parallel and tensor-parallel layout that fills 32 GPUs, probed up a session-lane ladder and refined one engine knob at a time — 252 runs, 36 servable finalists, 0 shapes the simulator refused or that missed the floor.

This is a prefill-dominated workload: 90,449 input tokens per request against 916 output, about 99:1. Output tok/s per GPU reads low by chatbot standards because almost all the work is reading context — the winner is ingesting roughly 144,666 input tok/s.
8x TP4 + EP at 102 concurrent agent sessions (80% of the measured ceiling of 128). Expert parallelism is not optional here: every non-EP control ran out of memory before serving a request.

meta: AgentX MVP replay (393 recorded Claude Code trajectories)
recommendation_prose: 8x TP4 + EP at 102 concurrent agent sessions, on the b200 deployment flags in the table below. That is 1,465.1 output tok/s across 32 GPUs (45.8 per GPU) at 131.4 tok/s per user and ITL p99 7.6 ms.
Leave the engine knobs at their defaults. None of the refinements helped, and the routing profiles in particular cost capacity on this traffic.

These are simulator predictions over a recorded corpus, not a live cluster measurement. The corpus is pinned by sha256, so the traffic is reproducible; the pricing is the blis-latency-kernel cost model and should be spot-checked against real serving data before anyone sizes a cluster from it.

sections.caption_note: The winner's ceiling is 128 lanes; the recommendation sits at 102, measured directly rather than interpolated.
prose: Throughput climbs almost linearly with lanes and then falls off a cliff. 8x TP4 + EP holds 115.0 tok/s per user at 128 lanes.
The cliff is why the recommendation is 102 lanes and not the ceiling: at the ceiling there is no headroom for a burst, and this workload's bursts are whole agent trajectories waking up at once.
sections.title: The operating curve, and where it stops

sections.caption_note: Both arms of each topology are shown where both were servable.
prose: Every expert-parallel candidate is run beside its non-EP control, so the direction is measured rather than assumed. On B200 the controls do run. Compared at a load both arms served, expert parallelism is worth between +0.0% and +10.9% — modest. Where it earns its place is capacity: it raises the servable ceiling, which is a different claim from being faster per token:

• 4x TP4xDP2 + EP: +10.9% at a matched 128 lanes (49.9 vs 45.0 tok/s/GPU)
  • 4x TP2xDP4 + EP: +7.4% at a matched 128 lanes (36.8 vs 34.2 tok/s/GPU)
  • 4x TP8 + EP: +3.8% at a matched 128 lanes (58.9 vs 56.8 tok/s/GPU)
  • 8x TP4 + EP: +2.5% at a matched 128 lanes (60.7 vs 59.2 tok/s/GPU)
  • 4x TP1xDP8 + EP: +0.0% at a matched 128 lanes (23.5 vs 23.5 tok/s/GPU)

It is worth contrasting that with the same search on a smaller-memory part: on a 79.2 GiB H100 no non-EP control survives at all. The difference is headroom — with 178.4 GiB per device the weights and a 256k-token KV pool fit without sharding the experts, so here EP is an optimisation rather than a precondition.

On this part the footprint stops binding altogether: no shape was refused, where the 79.2 GiB H100 run lost 12 of them to memory. What still separates the layouts is sharding width — the expert-parallel width is derived as tp × dp, so the narrow-TP arms shard nothing and scale badly.
sections.title: Expert parallelism helps here — but it is not what rescues the fit

sections.caption_note: Crosses are runs that missed the interactivity floor.
prose: Refinement moves one knob at a time off the winning topology, so any difference is attributable. Nothing improved on the defaults — these knobs constrain:

• batch tokens 2,048: 23.4 tok/s/GPU, -48.9% — and it halves usable capacity, C* 128 → 64
  • 1 draft token: 24.3 tok/s/GPU, -46.9% — and it halves usable capacity, C* 128 → 64
  • queue-kv routing: 25.0 tok/s/GPU, -45.4% — and it halves usable capacity, C* 128 → 64
  • gpu mem util 0.7: 25.4 tok/s/GPU, -44.5% — and it halves usable capacity, C* 128 → 64
  • 3 draft tokens: 25.9 tok/s/GPU, -43.4% — and it halves usable capacity, C* 128 → 64
  • 5 draft tokens: 26.8 tok/s/GPU, -41.5% — and it halves usable capacity, C* 128 → 64
  • max seqs 64: 45.9 tok/s/GPU, +0.2%
  • prefix-affinity routing: 45.9 tok/s/GPU, +0.2%

The expensive one is batch tokens 2,048 at -48.9%. It is not a small scheduling inefficiency: routing on queue depth and KV utilisation drops the servable ceiling from 128 lanes to 64, so the deployment loses half its capacity. Scoring on instantaneous KV pressure is actively wrong when every request arrives carrying ~90,449 tokens of context — the instance that looks least loaded is the one about to be handed an enormous prefill.
sections.title: The knobs that bind, and the one that really hurts

prose: This model ships its own drafter — the catalog graph declares a dspark speculator — so draft depth is a real deployment choice, not an exotic knob. Each depth is run against the no-drafting baseline on the winning topology:

• K=1: 24.3 tok/s/GPU, -6.2% against no drafting, acceptance length 1.81
  • K=3: 20.8 tok/s/GPU, -19.7% against no drafting, acceptance length 2.9
  • K=5: 27.0 tok/s/GPU, +4.2% against no drafting, acceptance length 3.51

Read those percentages carefully: each arm is scored at its own usable load, and drafting moves that load. A depth whose ceiling drops is therefore scored at a lower session count than the baseline, which makes it look worse than it is at any load they share — the matched-load table below is the comparison that answers “should I turn this on”. Here every depth holds the baseline’s 64-lane ceiling, so the figures above are already like-for-like.

How to read the per-user rate on these rows. Under drafting the engine reports the inter-token latency of a verification step, and one step emits as many tokens as the target accepts. So the per-user token rate is the acceptance length times 1000/ITL p99, not 1000/ITL p99 — the naive reading understates a drafting configuration by the whole acceptance factor and can make the fastest configuration measured look like a floor violation. The rows above use the acceptance-scaled rate, and the explorer labels it as derived.

At matched load, drafting is a clear throughput win — but it moves the interactivity cliff, so the two arms' own usable loads are not the same load. Output tok/s at each session count, with the change against no drafting:

The servable ceiling, however, falls: no drafting holds 64 lanes while K=1 at 64 lanes, K=3 at 64 lanes, K=5 at 64 lanes. Drafting spends decode compute verifying tokens, which is compute the baseline spends on concurrency — so the knob trades sessions for per-session speed. Set it from which of those you are short of: at a fixed session count below the drafting cliff it is close to free throughput, and above that cliff it costs you the sessions.
The acceptance lengths are measured, not assumed: they come from inferencex-golden-al (b200) in blis-registry, keyed by this model, drafter, depth, thinking mode and workload category.
sections.title: Speculative decoding, and what it does to the interactivity number

standfirst: A configuration search over 252 BLIS replay runs on 32× B200, driven by the recorded AgentX agentic traffic rather than a synthetic request shape. The winner is 8x TP4 + EP at 1,465.1 output tok/s (45.8 per GPU) while every user still reads at 131.4 tok/s.
title: Serving DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash to coding agents on 4 B200 nodes
